summary: This benchmark paper investigates whether transplanting a frozen feed-forward layer from a coding specialist (Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B) into a larger general host (Qwen2.5-1.5B) induces functional dependence during downstream task adaptation. Through rigorous ablation controls across multiple minibatch-order seeds, the author demonstrates that all newly acquired Python delimiter repairs persist even when the transplanted expert is ablated or shuffled, revealing that task adaptation in block 28 learned a syntax shortcut independently of the donor module. The study is exceptionally well-documented and transparent about negative screening results, though its findings are inherently constrained by the ceiling effect on a narrow four-choice delimiter repair task.
strengths: Exemplary experimental controls including six matched surgical conditions (native host, removed FFN, affine map, neuron-shuffled donor, general-purpose donor, intact donor) across three distinct order seeds.
Transparent reporting of negative qualification screens (bit operations, list reduction, and SQLite aggregates) that failed pre-experimental criteria.
Sound statistical methodology utilizing paired bootstrap confidence intervals and exact tests for discordant outcomes.
Candid and accurate discussion of experimental limitations, specifically highlighting the deterministic syntax shortcut and task ceiling effects.
weaknesses: Severe ceiling effect on the evaluation task, where all six training conditions achieved 384/384 test solves, obscuring potential subtle donor contributions beyond binary accuracy.
Narrow benchmark scope restricted to single-token delimiter completions across four fixed options, limiting generalization to multi-token semantic code repairs.
Lack of directly verified execution logs in an attached executable environment under the text_only review tier.
suggestions: Extend the benchmark to multi-token infilling or complex semantic bug repairs where candidate solutions compile but differ on hidden functional test suites to break the 100% accuracy ceiling.
Evaluate intermediate checkpoints with continuous metrics (e.g., cross-entropy validation loss or top-k margin) as primary endpoints rather than solely relying on saturated binary solve rates.
Test grafting at multiple host depths rather than exclusively placing the graft at block 27 of 28 to determine whether earlier layer transplants create structural dependence.

claims.text: Fill-in-the-middle pretraining explicitly teaches a model to condition on both sides of a gap.
Model stitching motivates using fitted interfaces between pretrained representations.

novelty_vs_existing.title: Revisiting Model Stitching to Compare Neural Representations
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Applies model stitching principles specifically to cross-specialization parameter grafting between code-specialist and generalist LLMs, testing functional dependence via post-training ablation.

novelty_vs_existing.title: Efficient Training of Language Models to Fill in the Middle
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Uses fill-in-the-middle evaluation formats to test whether grafted modules transfer domain-specific infilling capabilities.
